title: Report blames drugs, not Taser, for man's death
article: When Trevor Grimolfson was zapped three times with Tasers by police after storming through a pawnshop in a drug-addled fury in 2008, he had enough drugs in his system to kill him.

A report from the fatality inquiry into the death of the 38-year-old father and tattoo shop owner, states that it wasn't the Taser that caused his death - he had "very high levels" of MDMA (commonly called ecstasy) in his system, along with "very high levels" of Ketamine. There were also trace amounts of cocaine and an over-the-counter antihistamine.

"The level of MDMA (ecstasy) was sufficient to cause death by itself as was the level of Ketamine," wrote Judge Frederick Day in the report. "While excited delirium is the immediate cause of death, he would not be in excited delirium but for the presence of these levels of drugs."
On the morning of Oct. 29, 2008, Grimolfson assaulted the owner of a pawn shop on 153 Street and Stony Plain Road. Police were called.
Clifton Purvis, executive director of ASIRT, said when officers entered the store, Grimolfson was acting in a "highly agitated manner."
One of the officers zapped Grimolfson with his Taser after he refused to comply with orders to get down on the ground.
When Grimolfson headed towards the second officer, Purvis said his teeth and fist were clenched and his body was "vibrating." That officer deployed his Taser, but that too did not stop him.
A struggle ensued with two cops before the Taser was deployed again in Grimolfson 's neck, but showed no effect.

The two officers eventually restrained Grimolfson. He continued to struggle briefly after being restrained, but within minutes, he was unresponsive. He was taken to hospital where he was declared dead.
In 2009, the medical examiner determined that Grimolfson 's death was caused by excited delirium due to multiple drug toxicity.

Excited delirium is a relatively uncommon condition known to strike drug and alcohol abusers. Victims typically display aggressive, paranoid behaviour that's combined with "superhuman" strength that can take between six and eight people to restrain.
What is critical to assess, Day wrote in his two-page report, is the time of last use of the Taser and the time of unconsciousness.

"If it is within 15 seconds, then the Taser use could be a contributor to the cause of death, but, if it is outside 15 seconds, then the probability that Taser use was a contributor to cause of death is negligible," wrote Day.
"Here, a few minutes passed, not seconds, from the time of last Taser use to time of unconsciousness; therefore, the Taser use is not a relevant factor."
